clue.text: Warlike nation in fight with soldiers

parts.note: to spar is to fight, as boxers do in training
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve soldiers

explanation.surface: A belligerent country goes to war backed by its troops.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek city-state was famed for its military discipline and warrior culture.

clue.text: Hoping initially to get in shoot, with nothing in print

indicators.note: to get in says that letter is placed inside the word for shoot

parts.note: to pot is to shoot, as in taking a potshot at game

indicators.note: initially asks for only the opening letter of the word Hoping

parts.note: O, the round zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: A hopeful photographer wants to get a shot with nothing in the picture yet.
explanation.definitionFit: A photographic print is a picture developed on paper, the everyday snapshot.

clue.text: Evidence of lack of work that is around cool guy, leading to ban from college

parts.note: metal left unused gathers rust, a sign it has not been working

indicators.note: around says the letters for that is wrap themselves round the cool guy

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is
a cat is jazz slang for a cool fellow

explanation.surface: An idle student, plainly not working and too cool to care, ends up sent down.
explanation.walkthrough: In British universities, especially Oxford and Cambridge, to be rusticated is to be sent away from college for a period as a punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: Rusticating a student means suspending them from their university for a set time, a disciplinary exclusion.

clue.text: A play about robots involving second coating of metal

indicators.note: involving says the play's letters take in the word for second

parts.note: R.U.R. is Karel Čapek's 1920 play which introduced the word robot
a mo is a moment, a second, as in wait a mo

explanation.surface: A science-fiction drama about machines briefly covers metal plating.
explanation.definitionFit: Armour is protective metal plating, the casing covering a knight or a tank.

clue.text: I brought in books (University left us holding nothing) ready to drink in volumes

indicators.note: brought in says the letter I is placed inside the books

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for book, so two of them make books

indicators.note: holding says the preceding letters clasp the word for nothing within them

parts.note: O, the round zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: A student hauls in a pile of library books, then leaves; the scholar keen to drink in whole volumes.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's 'drink in volumes' suggests reading avidly; the definition really means drinking alcohol in large quantities.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone bibulous is fond of alcohol, always ready to down large amounts of liquor.

clue.text: Uninspired actors in broadcast of single setting of comic novels

parts.note: bland means dull, uninspired

indicators.note: in says the company of performers sits inside the rearranged letters
broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters of single are strewn into a new order

parts.note: the cast of a play is its actors

explanation.surface: Dull performers appear in a broadcast of a lone comedy series.
explanation.walkthrough: Blandings Castle is the stately home in P. G. Wodehouse's comic stories featuring Lord Emsworth and his prize pig.
explanation.definitionFit: Wodehouse set a long series of humorous novels at this fictional Shropshire stately home.

clue.text: Feature of pub, with busy person behind, bearing first of pints

parts.note: a busy bee is a proverbially industrious worker

indicators.note: bearing says the backside carries the next letter within it

parts.note: behind is a word for the backside, the rump

indicators.note: first of asks for the opening letter of pints

explanation.surface: A busy barman behind the counter pulls the first pints in a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: The handle on a bar used to draw real ale from the cellar is a standard fixture of a British pub.

clue.text: Book that's put in fake story initially liable for this?

definitions.text: Book that's put in fake story initially liable for this?

indicators.note: put in says the letter for book goes inside the word for a fake story

parts.note: a lie is a fabricated story

indicators.note: initially asks for only the opening letter of liable

explanation.surface: A book containing a false tale might leave its author open to a lawsuit.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a published book with a false, damaging story is what courts call this.
explanation.definitionFit: A defamatory statement in print is the tort for which a publisher of a false story can be sued.

clue.text: Dean and Court rubbished first application

indicators.note: rubbished means wrecked or trashed, so the letters of the two names are scrambled

explanation.surface: A dean dismisses a court's initial filing as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First application' looks legal, like a court submission, but it is about decorating.
explanation.definitionFit: Painters lay down a preliminary coat before the topcoat, so it is the first layer applied.

clue.text: Study everything — end of game should be perfect

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
the sum is the whole, everything added up
mate, or checkmate, ends a game of chess

explanation.surface: Review everything you know, and the final move of the match should be flawless.
explanation.definitionFit: Consummate as an adjective means complete or supremely skilled, flawless in every respect.

clue.text: Government abandoning move in seaside resort

indicators.note: abandoning says that letter is dropped from the next word

parts.note: to budge is to move, shift slightly

explanation.surface: Ministers refuse to shift policy on a coastal town.
explanation.walkthrough: Bude is a small seaside town on the north coast of Cornwall in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: This Cornish town is a surfing and holiday spot on the Atlantic coast, a resort by the sea.

clue.text: Bone in tumulus showing indication of death

indicators.note: in says the bone sits inside the burial heap

parts.note: a tumulus is an ancient burial mound
a rib is one of the bones of the chest

explanation.surface: A bone found in an ancient barrow is a sign of a death long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: Moribund describes something at the point of death, visibly dying or declining.

clue.text: Friend's bash, not very lavish

parts.note: a pal is a friend
to have a bash is to have a try

explanation.surface: A mate's party turns out to be a rather stingy affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bash' looks like a party, but it means an attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Paltry means meagre or trifling, the opposite of generous or extravagant.

clue.text: Instrument engaged in rolling over, knocking out rear of piano

indicators.note: rolling over says what remains is turned round and read backwards
knocking out says a letter is removed from the word for engaged in

parts.note: to be about something is to be engaged in it, as in going about your work

indicators.note: rear of asks for the final letter of piano

explanation.surface: A musician busy rolling about knocks the back off a piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking out' drops O from ABOUT, leaving ABUT, which 'rolling over' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: The tuba is the large, deep-voiced brass wind instrument of the orchestra.

clue.text: Everyone agreeing international group's elevated in blocking friendship

parts.note: UN is the United Nations, an international body

indicators.note: blocking says the turned little word sits inside the word for friendship, obstructing it

parts.note: amity is friendship, peaceful goodwill

indicators.note: elevated, in a down clue, says the little word in is written upwards

explanation.surface: A world body raised its voice to stop a friendship, and everyone agreed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'international group's' reads as a possessive, but the 's is simply joining it to the rest of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Unanimity is complete agreement, a state where all parties share the same view.

clue.text: Pardon me, if moved to affect importance

indicators.note: moved means shifted about, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone apologises for pushing past, affecting an air of self-importance.
explanation.definitionFit: Name-dropping means casually mentioning famous acquaintances to make yourself seem important.

clue.text: Panel of motorists to frustrate directors

parts.note: to dash hopes is to frustrate them
a company's directors form its board

explanation.surface: A committee of drivers sets out to thwart a company's executives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Panel of motorists' reads as a committee, but it is the instrument panel in a car.
explanation.definitionFit: The fascia in front of a driver holding the gauges and controls is a panel every car owner knows.

clue.text: Female carnivore digested no end of liver

indicators.note: digested means broken down, so the remaining letters are rearranged
no says the following letter is to be absent from the meat-eater's letters
end of asks for the final letter of liver

explanation.surface: A meat-eater swallowed a liver almost whole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end of liver' drops R from CARNIVORE, and 'digested' rearranges CANIVORE.
explanation.definitionFit: Veronica is a woman's given name, so it is a female forename.

clue.text: Nonchalant expression of affection ensnares the French

indicators.note: ensnares says the touch traps the French article within it

parts.note: a caress is a loving stroke or touch
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A tender embrace captures a casual French charm.
explanation.definitionFit: Careless here means casual or unconcerned, showing no worry, just as nonchalant does.

clue.text: Ill-feeling in hiding piano's location

indicators.note: in hiding says the musical letter goes out of sight, removed from the word

parts.note: spite is malice, ill-feeling
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly

explanation.surface: Bad blood leads someone to hide the piano and keep its whereabouts secret.
explanation.definitionFit: A site is a place or position where something is situated.

clue.text: Bob, say, cheated on love, suppressing a lot of passion

indicators.note: on, in a down clue, says the first piece sits on top of the next
suppressing says the outer letters hold down the trimmed passion inside

parts.note: to be had is to be cheated or conned

indicators.note: a lot of means not all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: ire is anger, a fiery passion
love is zero in tennis, written O

explanation.surface: Bob was unfaithful to his love, keeping most of his passion in check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a man's name; it is a short haircut, so 'say' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A bob is a style of haircut, so it is one example of a hairstyle.

clue.text: It provided backing before company failure

indicators.note: backing says the two preceding words' letters are written backwards

parts.note: It means sex appeal, abbreviated SA
if means provided that

explanation.surface: It gave financial support before a firm collapsed.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiasco is a humiliating flop, a complete and ludicrous failure.

clue.text: Demand to include black — described thus?

indicators.note: to include says the word for demand takes the letter for black inside it

parts.note: sale means demand, as in a product with a ready sale
B is the pencil abbreviation for black

explanation.surface: Someone insists that black be put in, and asks if that is the way to describe it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points back at 'black': the heraldic word for the colour black is the answer, so black is described thus.
explanation.definitionFit: Sable is the term for black in heraldry and poetry, the way that colour is named.

clue.text: A location of intimacies in woman's novel

indicators.note: in says the bed is placed within the word for woman

parts.note: a dame is a woman
a bed is where intimacies take place

explanation.surface: A setting for intimate moments appears in a female author's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at the author: George Eliot, who wrote this 1859 novel, was the woman Mary Ann Evans.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam Bede is George Eliot's first full-length work of fiction, set in rural England.

clue.text: Some received it today, just as before

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some people got it today, the same as last time.
explanation.definitionFit: Ditto means the same again, used to repeat what was said or written previously.

clue.text: Member showing absence of progress, nothing less

indicators.note: less means minus, so that letter is taken away

parts.note: to be in limbo is to be stuck, making no progress
O, the round zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: A club member is shown stalled, with nothing to show for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A limb is an arm or leg, a member of the body in the older sense of that word.

clue.text: Fashionable Father excited about it, being ecumenical

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in the in thing

indicators.note: about says the jumbled letters go round the little word it
excited means stirred up, so the letters of Father are rearranged

explanation.surface: A trendy priest is thrilled about church unity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' rearranges FATHER into TERFAH, which goes 'about' IT.
explanation.definitionFit: An interfaith gathering brings different religions together, the spirit of a church unity movement.

clue.text: Appearance of text borders on totally precise — fellow's excellent

indicators.note: borders on asks for the first and last letters of each of the next two words

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow
ace means excellent

explanation.surface: The text looks entirely exact, and the chap says it's first-rate.
explanation.definitionFit: A font or typeface determines how printed text looks on the page, its design.

clue.text: Implausible item in musical getting cut? Very likely

parts.note: odd means strange, hard to credit

indicators.note: getting cut says the word is shortened, losing its final letter

parts.note: a song is a number in a musical

explanation.surface: A far-fetched number in a show is likely to be dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Odds-on describes a betting favourite, more likely to win than lose, so almost certain.
